courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: The paper calls r = 1 necessary but not sufficient: an agent that issues the correct return *without* asking for confirmation still scores 1, even though it broke policy. Database comparison catches wrong outcomes, not bad conduct along the way.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Permissions, traces and evaluation
md: Permission checks are only as strong as the sandbox behind them. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments for agents; run untrusted or autonomous agents in a container or VM with limited network and credentials, and reserve modes that skip approval for those isolated environments.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Misconception: if the agent ran the tests itself and reported success, the work is verified. The report is model output, and tests the agent wrote or could edit are not independent. Run the checks in the harness, on a clean copy, with tests the agent did not control.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
md: Treat the environment as part of the training algorithm. Its reward defines what is learned, its isolation defines what can be cheated, and its throughput (containers times 3600 divided by episode seconds) defines how many steps you can afford.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
md: A text watermark is a keyed, pseudorandom preference applied at sampling time. Detection re-derives the preference from the text and asks whether the text agrees with it far more often than chance.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
md: What interposition misses: statically linked programs (LD_PRELOAD is a feature of the dynamic linker), secure-execution binaries (the linker ignores LD_PRELOAD paths with slashes), and any memory that bypasses malloc: direct mmap, custom arenas and pools, GPU allocations. heaptrack's README notes pool allocators need code annotations to be profiled.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Testing input types on your own data
md: Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
md: The future contract: **if `poll` returns `Pending`, the future must make sure the waker from that call gets woken later** when progress is possible. Forget it and the task hangs forever, with no error. The Tokio tutorial calls this a common source of bugs.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses
md: Use the most specific operation that does the job. If a fetch_add, fetch_or or swap expresses your update, prefer it to a hand-written CAS loop: it never fails, and on ARM the compiler turns it into a tight instruction sequence, which (as of Mara Bos's tests) it does not do for a hand-written CAS loop.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
md: More subagents is not automatically better. Anthropic's early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and distracted each other with updates. Their prompts now embed effort rules: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3 to 10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each, and complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Specific burndown rates, default quotas and tier prices change as models launch. Treat any number you remember as stale and read the current quota page and model card before you size a workload.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
md: Agner Fog's rule of thumb: a conditional jump beats a conditional move when the code is part of a dependency chain and prediction is better than about 75 percent. For random binary-search keys (about 50 percent) cmov wins; for keys that cluster, the branch wins.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
md: A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
md: Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: Arrange data so that what you use together sits together, and walk it in address order. Stride 1 is the cheapest pattern there is.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: EM can only separate rank from document if the same documents appear at different ranks, and those overlaps must link all ranks together. When ranker 2 was D, E, B, A, C instead, ranks {1, 4} and {2, 3, 5} never shared a document, the relative scale between the two groups was unidentifiable, and EM's answer for rank 2 depended on its starting point: 0.63 starting from 0.5, 0.53 starting from 0.3 (truth 0.5).

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Lloyd's algorithm by hand, and why the seeds decide
md: k-means++ is the only step here with a guarantee. Arthur and Vassilvitskii prove $E[\phi] \le 8(\ln k + 2)\,\phi_{OPT}$ after seeding alone, before a single Lloyd iteration; the iterations can then only lower it. In scikit-learn `init="k-means++"` is the default (a greedy variant that tries several candidates per step), and `n_init="auto"` means 1 run with k-means++ but 10 runs with `init="random"`.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: From tuple-at-a-time to vector-at-a-time execution
md: Vectorization keeps the iterator model but changes its unit from one tuple to a cache-sized vector. That amortizes interpretation overhead (small n is bad) without materializing whole columns in RAM (huge n is bad).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
md: Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Grounding: Set-of-Mark labels, DOM and accessibility trees
md: Misconception: Set-of-Mark always improves GUI grounding. Both SeeAct and OSWorld saw marks underperform richer text grounding on dense screens. Marks help most when there are few, well-separated elements.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Preemption bounds, weak memory and what loom cannot see
md: Known gaps, from the loom README: `SeqCst` loads and stores are treated as `AcqRel`, which is weaker, so loom can raise **false alarms** on code that relies on SeqCst (`fence(SeqCst)` is supported). And loom does not explore **load buffering**, where a later store becomes visible to an earlier load, so it can **miss bugs**. loom is neither fully sound nor fully complete for C11.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: A central lookup table (key range to server) also gives minimal movement, and many databases use one. The catch is that every client must fetch and agree on the table. Consistent hashing lets each client compute the owner from the key and the server list alone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
md: A missing field scores **1**, the best possible decay value, in both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Profiles with no location beat everyone who lives a few kilometers away. Decide explicitly: require the field with an `exists` filter, index a default value, or accept the behavior on purpose.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: Common mistakes. **CP-SAT works over integers only**: a coefficient like 0.5 must be scaled (multiply the constraint by 2). A status of `FEASIBLE` after a time limit is not a proof of optimality, and `UNKNOWN` is not a proof of infeasibility. With more than one worker, runs are not guaranteed to be repeatable; tests and demos often set `num_workers = 1`.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Let the LLM decide **what changed**; let code decide **what the state is** and **what the query is**. This split makes carryover free, makes every change visible in logs, and turns the hardest part into a small, testable classification problem.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
md: Each test rules out one failure class, nothing more. A CoT that passes truncation and mistake tests is causally used, but it can still omit a factor (as in Turpin's hints). Lanham et al. call this a defense-in-depth approach: no single test certifies faithfulness.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A bi-encoder pays the document cost once, offline. A cross-encoder pays the full transformer cost for every (query, document) pair at query time. That single fact explains both why it is more accurate and why it can only rerank a shortlist.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: More stages are not automatically faster. Each stage costs shared memory that a bigger tile or a smem-staged epilogue could use, and once loads are hidden, extra stages add nothing. StageCountAuto simply fills what is left.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions
md: Pick the memory zone deliberately. Hot-plugged CXL memory can be onlined as `ZONE_MOVABLE` or `ZONE_NORMAL`. Kernel allocations are generally not migratable and can only use `ZONE_NORMAL` or lower, so CXL memory in `ZONE_MOVABLE` serves only user pages and other movable data. `daxctl` onlines as movable by default; that keeps kernel data off the device but means CXL capacity cannot absorb kernel memory pressure.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: Think in two levels. **Within** a domain, filter documents (deduplicate, drop low-quality pages with a classifier). **Across** domains, choose weights with a method like DoReMi or a fitted mixing model. Then rerun the mixing step, because filtering changes each domain's size and difficulty.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: List the hot loops, write down which fields each one touches and whether it streams or jumps, then pick the layout that packs those bytes together. Re-measure when the access pattern changes.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: DST turns rare, timing-dependent bugs into seeds. The engineering cost is up front (every source of nondeterminism behind an interface, plus good oracles), and the return is that every bug found is a bug you can replay and fix.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Misconception: "interference only matters at high load." In the timeline there was just one new prompt. Any long prompt that lands in a decode iteration creates a stall for every request in the batch. Load makes it more frequent, not possible.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
md: Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
md: Do not read DPO's $\beta$ as a guarantee of staying close to the reference. On pairs the model already separates, DPO's gradient shrinks but never pushes back, so drift continues as long as you keep training. The IPO paper notes that early stopping is the usual extra guard.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
md: A backfill copy is always an *old* view of a row. Whatever mechanism you use (insert-if-absent, versions, or watermarks), it must guarantee that a backfilled row can never land after a newer write for the same key, and that deletes are remembered.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
md: Probe context matters. `tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue` often fires in the context of the process that issued the I/O, but it can also fire from kernel context (for example readahead), so `comm` and `pid` may not name the application you expect.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
md: Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: Real aggregates are not the clean sum of the appliances you know about. UK-DALE reports that in House 1, with monitors on almost every appliance, only 80% of the energy was sub-metered, partly because the 52 plug monitors themselves draw about 50 W. The $\varepsilon_t$ term is never zero.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
md: Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: Readiness is a hint, not a promise. The [select(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/select.2.html) page warns that a socket can be reported readable and a following read can still block, for example when the arrived packet had a bad checksum and was dropped. That is why event loops always use nonblocking sockets.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results
md: ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
md: FP8 FlashAttention-3 was released for the forward pass only (FP16 and BF16 have forward and backward), and the paper's FP8 kernel lacked the persistent-kernel load balancing of the FP16 one, so it trailed cuDNN's FP8 kernels for short sequences and causal masking. It reached close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s, about 60% of an FP8 peak taken as twice the FP16 peak.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Durable means: the bytes reached stable media **and** everything needed to find them (file size, block map, directory entry) did too. `write()` gives you neither; `fsync()` on the file and its directory gives you both.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
md: `partial_ratio` produces false positives on short strings: `fuzz.partial_ratio("ai", "said hello")` is 100 because `ai` appears inside `said`. Likewise `token_set_ratio` returns 100 for any subset, so `google` vs `google cloud platform team` is a perfect score. Use these scorers with a minimum length or combine them with other evidence.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: The verification math assumes stray detections are independent and uniform. Satellite trails, diffraction spikes, plate scratches and dense clusters violate that, so false positives there are far more common than the formula predicts. Mask streaks before solving.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: All three systems are the same idea as lesson 3: name cells with integers, cover the query with cells, read those cells, then refine. S2 and H3 trade geohash's simplicity for cells that behave well everywhere on the sphere, including poles and the antimeridian.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Misconception: "OOM with lots of reserved memory means a leak." Often it is fragmentation: the free memory exists but in holes smaller than the request, inside segments that cannot be released because a live tensor still occupies part of them.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: **Misconception:** coalescing requires thread k to read element k. It does not. The Programming Guide notes that permuted access within the same 32-byte segments is just as good. What matters is the ratio of bytes used to bytes transferred.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: Remember the order. The timeline sets the denominator for everything else: a kernel that is 4 percent of the wall time can never give you more than 4 percent, however bad its counters look.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
md: SIMT is not the same as SIMD. In CPU SIMD the software sees the vector width and manages lanes itself. In SIMT you write scalar per-thread code and the hardware groups it. Correctness never depends on warps; performance does, much like cache lines.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
md: Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: RLVR changes where the reward comes from, not the RL algorithm. Tulu 3 ran RLVR with PPO; DeepSeek ran it with GRPO. The rest of this course is about GRPO, the algorithm that made RLVR cheap at scale.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
md: With FULL_DATASET, each fetch is the entire current state. If a trip's update was in the last message but is missing from this one, the consumer must treat it as having no realtime data now, and the reference is explicit that no TripUpdate does **not** mean the trip is on time.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
md: A sound counter workflow: `perf stat` for IPC and TopdownL1, drill into the biggest bucket with grouped metrics, then `perf record` on the matching event with `:pp` to find the code, change it, and measure again.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
md: RRF is not parameter-free. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023) showed that NDCG swings noticeably when the per-retriever constants are changed, and that constants tuned in-domain did not transfer reliably out of domain. Also, the window size is a hidden parameter: a document at rank 11 with a window of 10 contributes nothing at all.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Rejecting bad matches, warping, and direct ECC alignment
md: Those border zeros look like a dark region in the warped image, and subtracting it from the reference flags a band of fake change along the edges. Warp an all-ones image with the same H to get a validity mask, and ignore pixels outside it.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: A classic bug: `char buf[4096];` on the stack of a function that preps a read, submits, and returns. The kernel later writes 4096 bytes into a stack frame that now belongs to someone else. Buffers belong to the kernel from submission until the matching CQE.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency and RSS on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
md: The search space is a product, so it grows exponentially in the number of knobs and linearly in the number of shapes you tune for. Any plan that says "just benchmark them all" has to survive that product.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
md: No IOMMU, no safety. `uio_pci_generic`, `igb_uio` and VFIO's `enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode` let the device DMA to any physical address. A bug in the application then corrupts the kernel or other processes: the ixy authors report losing a filesystem to rogue DMA writes on a misconfigured server. DPDK recommends vfio-pci with the IOMMU enabled.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
md: Epilogue fusion matters less than elementwise fusion for big GEMMs: the matmul is compute bound and dominates, so removing a 66 us kernel from a 947 us layer saves about 7 percent. It matters more for small or skinny matmuls, where the GEMM itself is short.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
md: Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
md: Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
md: In production, LambdaMART is the training objective of a tree ensemble that rescores the top candidates of a first-stage retriever. Its quality depends on labels (judgments or debiased clicks), query-grouped data, and a truncation level that matches the positions users see.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
md: LLM-as-judge for relevance is a measurement instrument. Like any instrument, you calibrate it against a trusted reference (human gold labels) before you read numbers off it.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
md: Do not rank by raw win percentage when models faced different opponents: beating weak models inflates it. BT accounts for who played whom. And never report a ranking without intervals; with few votes, neighbouring models are often statistically tied.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Never match binary descriptors with Euclidean (L2) distance on their byte values. A byte of 10000000 and one of 01111111 are 1 apart as numbers but differ in all 8 bits. OpenCV's matching tutorial says to use `cv.NORM_HAMMING` for ORB, BRIEF and BRISK, and `cv.NORM_L2` (the default) for SIFT.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank, so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: "Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: Start from the happens-before edges your algorithm needs, then pick the weakest ordering that creates each one. Mara Bos suggests treating SeqCst as a warning sign in review: it claims dependence on the order of every SeqCst operation in the program, which is much harder to verify than a single Release/Acquire pair.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU readers pay almost nothing; updaters copy, publish with one pointer store, and defer the free until a grace period has elapsed. A grace period waits only for readers that started before the removal.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: Union and RRF are not interchangeable. A union returns everything (N x k documents at worst) in retrieval order, so taking its first k usually just returns the first query's list. Pick RRF when the next stage has a fixed budget; pick union when a reranker will score all candidates anyway.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
md: **Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
md: Shampoo and SOAP are often called *second-order*, but they do not compute the Hessian. Like AdaGrad and Adam, they build preconditioners from products of gradients ($GG^\top$ and $G^\top G$).

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muP is not a formula that predicts the best SP learning rate for a bigger model. It changes how every layer's init and update scale with width, so a wide muP model trains differently from (and in the paper's experiments, better than) a wide SP model.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield`. It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
md: Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: NeMo RL separates *what the algorithm does* (a single-controller loop written as if on one GPU) from *where it runs* (RayVirtualCluster plus RayWorkerGroups). Swapping vLLM for another engine, or changing GPU counts, should not change the algorithm code.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
md: Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
md: The AP number picks the model; the confidence threshold, chosen on validation data that looks like deployment, decides how it behaves.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: The shape of the data decides which questions you can ask. Metrics answer "how often, how slow, for everyone". Traces answer "where did the time go inside this one request". Logs answer "what exactly happened at this instant".

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: A dashboard is an ordered list of questions, not a list of metrics. Start with the SLO burn rate (are users hurt), then symptoms (what is broken), then causes and changes (why), then one link into a single trace (prove it).

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS = average over questions of the best (1 minus normalized edit distance) against any ground truth, zeroed when the distance reaches 0.5. It rewards nearly right reading, not semantic equivalence.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
md: Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
md: Do not reorder blindly. If a struct's layout is part of a file format, a network protocol, a hardware register map or an ABI shared with other code, changing the order changes the bytes and breaks every reader. Reordering is safe only for structs that are private to one build of your program.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
md: Monte Carlo labels estimate a **value** (the chance this policy finishes correctly from here), not step correctness. Qwen's 2025 study argues this is the core flaw: a correct step can score low because the completer is weak, and a wrong step can score high because the completer repairs it. They found MC-labeled PRMs worse than ones trained on LLM-as-a-judge or human labels at locating errors.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
md: More sampling buys you less than independence suggests. Sequence sampling cannot rescue an undesignable backbone, which is why designability of the generator, measured at a fixed small M, is the metric the backbone papers compete on.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
md: Pick the pattern by the question's shape: a vague or context-dependent question needs one **rewrite**; a chain of facts needs **sequential decomposition** (Self-Ask, IRCoT); an over-specific question benefits from a **step-back**; a question that could be phrased many ways benefits from **multi-query** fan-out.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
md: Majorities intersect. Every safety argument in Paxos and Raft comes down to one server that sat in both quorums and remembered what it saw.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
md: Three separate decisions shape the context: **how many** chunks (top-k), **how many tokens** they may use (the budget, set by the window minus everything else), and **in what order** they appear. Tune them together; raising k without a budget or an ordering rule mostly adds noise to the middle.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
md: Filling a missing value with 0 is safe only when 0 already means the worst value. For a feature like 1/window it does. For a z-scored feature, 0 means average, so a missing value silently becomes an average document. Use the worst observed value (LETOR's MIN approach) or add a separate is-missing flag.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
md: RDMA is not "the OS is gone". The kernel driver still creates queues, pins and maps memory, and handles errors. What disappears is per-message kernel work. That split between a slow **control path** and a fast **data path** is the design of the whole API.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
md: An authoritative server makes the server state the only truth. Every latency trick in the next lessons changes only what the *client displays*; none of them lets a client decide the outcome.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference
md: A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: The reward is an imperfect measurement of the goal. Optimization pressure flows to wherever the measurement and the goal disagree, so the harder you optimize, the more those disagreements decide what you get.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
md: Partial rollouts are not free. A trajectory stitched from segments generated by several policy versions is off-policy data. Kimi notes some segments can be excluded from the loss; AReaL's interruptible rollouts face the same issue and handle it with a modified PPO objective.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Placing GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on the roofline
md: Intensity is not fixed for a given operation. It depends on shape (thin GEMMs fall left), precision (FP8 halves the bytes per element and so doubles intensity), and how well the implementation reuses data. A naive GEMM that rereads inputs from DRAM can be memory bound even at 8192 cubed.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: An RRF score is not a relevance probability. Its size depends on k and on how many lists were fused (Azure AI Search notes each query contributes at most about $1/k$), so do not apply a fixed threshold to it across queries or configurations.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Misconception: "Rust drivers do not need cleanup code." They need exactly as much cleanup as C drivers. The difference is that it lives once in a `Drop` impl (yours or an abstraction's) and runs on every path automatically, including early returns from `?`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
md: Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
md: They stack. Check the semantic cache first; on a miss, send a request whose stable content comes first so the provider's prefix cache can reuse it. Prompt caching is safe to turn on everywhere; a semantic cache needs the threshold and scoping work from the previous lessons.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
md: All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: A non-NULL return from `malloc` does not mean the memory exists. Under default overcommit a large allocation succeeds immediately, and the failure, if any, comes later as an OOM kill when the pages are first written, far from the line that allocated them.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Per-partition order is *write* order, not event-time order. If sensor A's readings were written late (e12 in our toy), they sit in the log after newer ones. Kafka removes the network chaos between bridge and processor, but it cannot undo disorder that happened before the write.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: Attention did not start with the Transformer. Additive attention over RNN states dates to Bahdanau et al. (2014). What was new in 2017 was using attention *alone*, with no recurrence or convolution.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
md: BM25 is still a sum over query terms of (IDF) x (a term-frequency factor). What changes is the term-frequency factor: it is bounded and length-aware instead of a raw count.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
md: The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: $f'(x)$ answers: if I nudge $x$ by a tiny amount, how many times that amount does $f$ change? Positive means $f$ rises to the right, negative means it falls, zero means the tangent is flat.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
md: A command runs in a **copy** of the shell. It inherits open files, the working directory and exported variables, and nothing it changes flows back. Only builtins and functions run inside the shell itself.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
md: An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Every malloc needs exactly one matching free, on every path out of the function. Missing it leaks memory; doing it twice, or touching the block afterwards, is undefined behavior that can corrupt the allocator's own bookkeeping.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta$. Its sign says whether two vectors point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero), or opposite (negative). Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: The loss you minimize is computed on the **training** data, but what you actually care about is performance on new data. Lessons 4 and 5 show how these two come apart.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
md: The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout: train mode vs eval mode
md: BatchNorm and Dropout behave **differently in train and eval mode**. `model.train()` and `model.eval()` flip that switch for every such layer at once; forgetting either one is among the most common silent bugs in practice.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (branch speculation control) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
md: Total experience is the length of the union of role intervals, not the sum of their lengths. Sort by start, sweep, extend with max of the ends, and record gaps as you close blocks.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Surprise is not a separate score or probability the model predicts. It is the inner-loss gradient itself, the same quantity a TTT step already uses. Likewise $\eta_t$ here is momentum *inside the memory's inner loop*; it has nothing to do with the outer optimizer (AdamW) that trains the network.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: Fusion in Triton is mostly a matter of keeping a tile in registers between operations. Load once, do every elementwise op and reduction on the block, store once.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: GenEval prompts are short and templated, and some models are trained mostly on long synthetic captions. Emu3's authors say exactly this and report rewriter numbers too. Before comparing two papers, check the rewriter, the CFG scale, and whether numbers were measured or copied from another paper.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Durability comes from the log, not the index: indexes are rebuilt or replayed from the WAL. Speed comes from what fits in RAM: keep the navigation data (graph upper layers, compressed vectors) in memory, and make every disk read count.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
